BACK & SPINE__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Why this matters: back pain is one of the commonest presentations in medicine — and hides emergencies (cauda equina, cord compression, infection, malignancy). This subtab ties the spine together into the disc prolapse, radiculopathy, the red flags and lumbar puncture you’ll be examined on and will meet on the wards.
Back Pain & Red Flags
Mechanical (most common)
  • Worse on movement, better with rest; no systemic features; muscular/ligamentous or degenerative (spondylosis)
Red flags → investigate
  • Cauda equina — saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral sciatica
  • Malignancy — age >50, weight loss, night pain, past cancer
  • Infection — fever, IVDU, immunosuppression (discitis/epidural abscess)
  • Fracture — trauma, osteoporosis, steroids
  • Inflammatory — young, morning stiffness >30 min, better with exercise (ankylosing spondylitis)
Intervertebral Disc Prolapse & Radiculopathy
Mechanism
  • The nucleus pulposus herniates through a torn annulus fibrosus, usually posterolaterally (the posterior longitudinal ligament is strong centrally)
  • It compresses the traversing (lower) nerve root — e.g. an L4/5 disc typically hits the L5 root
Common levels
  • L4/5 disc → L5 root: weak big-toe extension (EHL), numb dorsum of foot, walking on heels difficult
  • L5/S1 disc → S1 root: weak plantarflexion, numb sole/lateral foot, reduced ankle jerk
Sciatica is radicular leg pain in a dermatomal pattern; the straight-leg-raise (Lasègue’s) test reproduces it (L5/S1), while the femoral stretch test targets higher roots (L2–L4).
Cauda Equina Syndrome
Why it happens
  • The spinal cord ends at L1/L2 (conus medullaris); below that the cauda equina (lumbosacral roots) floats in CSF
  • A large central disc prolapse (or tumour/abscess) compresses these roots
Red-flag features
  • Saddle anaesthesia, painless urinary retention (then overflow), faecal incontinence/loss of anal tone
  • Bilateral sciatica & lower-limb weakness (LMN pattern)
Surgical emergency. Suspected cauda equina needs an urgent MRI and decompression — delay risks permanent bladder, bowel & sexual dysfunction.
Cord vs Cauda Equina — Localising the Lesion
FeatureCord (conus/above)Cauda equina
Neuron typeUMN (below the level)LMN
WeaknessSymmetrical, spasticAsymmetrical, flaccid
ReflexesHyperreflexia, up-going plantarsAreflexia, down-going
SensoryA sensory levelSaddle / dermatomal (roots)
SphinctersEarly — spastic (UMN) bladderLater — flaccid, retention
Spinal cord compression (e.g. metastasis) is also an emergency: back pain, a sensory level, UMN signs below and bladder involvement → urgent MRI whole spine & steroids.
Vertebral Fractures & Deformity
Fractures
  • Wedge/compression — osteoporotic (elderly, steroids); loss of anterior height
  • Burst — axial load; retropulsion of bone into the canal (can be unstable)
  • Chance — flexion-distraction (“seat-belt”); often with intra-abdominal injury
  • Stability depends on Denis’ three columns (anterior, middle, posterior)
Deformity
  • Kyphosis (excess thoracic flexion), lordosis (lumbar extension), scoliosis (lateral curve + rotation)
  • Spondylolisthesis — a vertebra slips forward on the one below
  • Spondylosis — degenerative disc/facet disease; spinal stenosis → neurogenic claudication
Lumbar Puncture & Spinal/Epidural Anaesthesia
Where & why
  • Performed at L3/L4 or L4/5 — below the conus (L1/2), so the needle meets only cauda equina roots (which move aside)
  • Tuffier’s line (between the iliac crests) marks the L4 spinous process (≈ the L4/5 interspace)
Layers pierced (to CSF)
  • Skin → superficial fascia → supraspinous → interspinous → ligamentum flavum → epidural (extradural) space → dura → arachnoid → subarachnoid space (CSF)
  • Spinal anaesthesia = into the CSF (subarachnoid); epidural = into the epidural space (no dural puncture)
Neural Tube Defects
Spina bifida occulta — a failed vertebral arch fusion only (a tuft of hair/dimple); usually asymptomatic.
Meningocele — meninges herniate through the defect (cord normal).
Myelomeningocele — meninges and neural tissue herniate → neurological deficit; associated with Chiari II & hydrocephalus.
Prevention — peri-conceptional folic acid; screened by a raised maternal AFP.
Clinical Signs & Roots
Straight-leg raise (Lasègue) — stretches the sciatic nerve (L5/S1 roots) → reproduces radicular pain.
Femoral stretch test — prone knee flexion → anterior-thigh pain (L2–L4 roots).
Key reflexes — knee jerk L3/4, ankle jerk S1; plantar up-going = UMN.
Dermatome anchors — nipple T4, umbilicus T10, groin L1, knee L3/4, big toe L5, little toe/sole S1.
🧠 Mnemonics
Cauda equina red flags — Saddle anaesthesia, Bladder/Bowel dysfunction, Bilateral sciatica → urgent MRI.
LP level — go below the conus (L1/2): L3/4 or L4/5 (Tuffier’s line = L4).
Disc rule — the disc hits the lower (traversing) root: L4/5 → L5; L5/S1 → S1.
“S1 = ankle jerk; L3/4 = knee jerk.”
⭐ Exam Pearls
Discs prolapse posterolaterally & hit the traversing root: L4/5 → L5, L5/S1 → S1.
Cauda equina = saddle anaesthesia + painless retention + bilateral sciatica → emergency MRI & decompression.
Cord ends at L1/L2 (conus); below is cauda equina — LP is done at L3/4 or L4/5.
Cord lesion = UMN + sensory level; cauda equina = LMN + saddle/root pattern.
Cord compression (mets) = back pain + sensory level + UMN signs → urgent MRI + steroids.
LP layers: supraspinous → interspinous → ligamentum flavum → dura → arachnoid → CSF.
Spinal = subarachnoid (CSF); epidural = epidural space (no dural puncture).
Osteoporotic wedge fractures lose anterior vertebral height; burst fractures can be unstable.
Myelomeningocele = cord + meninges herniate (deficit); prevented by folic acid.
SLR = L5/S1; femoral stretch = L2–L4.
BACK & SPINE__Osteology & Joints:
Why this matters: the vertebral column is a segmented pillar that bears weight, protects the cord and allows movement. Learn the regional vertebral features, the facet & craniovertebral joints and the spinal ligaments, and radiographs, fractures, disc disease and the “yes/no” head movements all make sense.
The Vertebral Column — Overview
33 vertebrae
  • 7 cervical · 12 thoracic · 5 lumbar · 5 fused sacral · 4 fused coccygeal (24 mobile presacral)
  • Separated by intervertebral discs; enclose the vertebral canal
Curvatures
  • Primary (kyphotic) — thoracic & sacral (present at birth, concave forward)
  • Secondary (lordotic) — cervical (holding the head up) & lumbar (walking), develop after birth
Structure of a Typical Vertebra
Parts
  • Body (anterior, weight-bearing) + vertebral arch (pedicles + laminae) → the vertebral foramen
  • Processes: one spinous, two transverse, and paired superior & inferior articular processes (facets)
Intervertebral foramen
  • Formed between the pedicles of adjacent vertebrae; transmits the spinal nerve (with its dorsal root ganglion) & radicular vessels
  • Narrowed by disc prolapse or osteophytes → radiculopathy
Regional Vertebrae
RegionBodyDistinctive features
CervicalSmallForamen transversarium (vertebral artery), bifid spinous (C3–6), triangular vertebral foramen
ThoracicHeart-shapedCostal facets/demifacets (rib heads) & transverse costal facets (tubercles); long, downward spinous
LumbarLarge, kidney-shapedNo costal facets/transverse foramina; short, blunt (“hatchet”) spinous; mamillary process
The atypical cervical vertebrae
  • Atlas (C1) — no body, no spinous process; anterior & posterior arches + lateral masses; facets for the occipital condyles
  • Axis (C2) — the dens (odontoid process), a pivot for the atlas
  • Vertebra prominens (C7) — long, non-bifid spinous (a surface landmark)
Sacrum & coccyx
  • Sacrum — 5 fused; the promontory, ala, anterior/posterior sacral foramina, median crest & sacral hiatus (caudal anaesthesia)
  • Coccyx — 4 fused rudimentary vertebrae
Joints of the Vertebral Column
Between the bodies
  • Intervertebral (symphysis) joints — secondary cartilaginous; the intervertebral disc = outer annulus fibrosus + inner nucleus pulposus (shock absorber)
  • Cervical uncovertebral joints (of Luschka) — small clefts that develop osteophytes
Between the arches
  • Zygapophyseal (facet) joints — synovial plane joints between the articular processes
  • Facet orientation sets the movement: cervical oblique (all movements), thoracic coronal (rotation, limited by ribs), lumbar sagittal (flexion/extension, little rotation)
The Craniovertebral Joints
Atlanto-occipital & atlanto-axial
  • Atlanto-occipital (C0–C1) — condylar synovial; flexion/extension → nodding “YES”
  • Atlanto-axial (C1–C2) — a pivot around the dens; rotation → shaking “NO” (~50% of neck rotation)
Key ligaments here
  • The transverse ligament of the atlas (part of the cruciate ligament) holds the dens against the anterior arch
  • Alar (dens → occipital condyles, limits rotation), apical, and the tectorial membrane (continuation of the PLL)
Danger. Rupture of the transverse ligament (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, trauma) or a fractured dens lets the dens compress the spinal cord — potentially fatal atlanto-axial instability.
Ligaments of the Spine
LigamentLocationLimits / role
Anterior longitudinalFront of the bodies (broad)Limits extension (the only one to do so)
Posterior longitudinalBack of the bodies (narrow)Limits flexion; directs discs posterolaterally
Ligamentum flavumBetween laminae (elastic)Resists flexion; pierced last before dura in LP
Interspinous / supraspinousBetween/over spinous processesLimit flexion
Ligamentum nuchaeCervical (supraspinous + interspinous)Muscle attachment & holds up the head
Movements & Applied Points
Cervical & lumbar regions are the most mobile; the thoracic spine is splinted by the ribs.
Jefferson fracture — a burst fracture of the C1 (atlas) ring from axial loading.
Hangman’s fracture — bilateral C2 pars/pedicle fracture (hyperextension).
Odontoid peg fracture — of the dens; risk of atlanto-axial instability.
Cervical rib — from C7; can cause thoracic outlet syndrome.
Sacralisation / lumbarisation — transitional L5/S1 anomalies.
🧠 Mnemonics
Vertebral count — 7-12-5-5-4 (breakfast 7, lunch 12, dinner 5…).
Atlas = YES, Axis = NO (atlanto-occipital nods; atlanto-axial rotates).
Foramen transversarium = a cervical vertebra (transmits the vertebral artery).
ALL limits extension; PLL limits flexion (Anterior/After = extension).
⭐ Exam Pearls
33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 4 coccygeal.
Primary curvatures (thoracic, sacral) = kyphotic; secondary (cervical, lumbar) = lordotic.
Foramen transversarium (vertebral artery) is unique to cervical vertebrae.
Atlas (C1) has no body/spinous; axis (C2) has the dens.
Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets/demifacets for the ribs.
IV disc = annulus fibrosus + nucleus pulposus; a secondary cartilaginous joint.
Facet (zygapophyseal) joints are synovial; their orientation sets regional movement.
Atlanto-occipital = “yes” (flexion/extension); atlanto-axial = “no” (rotation around the dens).
Transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens; its rupture → cord compression.
ALL limits extension; PLL (narrow) limits flexion & steers discs posterolaterally.
BACK & SPINE__Muscles & Movements:
Why this matters: the back muscles come in two families — the extrinsic (which actually move the upper limb) and the intrinsic (the true back muscles that move & stabilise the spine). The dividing rule is the nerve supply: intrinsic = posterior rami. Learn the layers, the erector spinae and the suboccipital triangle, and posture, back strain and the vertebral artery all make sense.
Two Groups of Back Muscles
Extrinsic (superficial)
  • Attach the upper limb / ribs to the axial skeleton — despite lying on the back, they move the limb or aid respiration
  • Supplied by anterior rami (or the accessory nerve for trapezius)
Intrinsic (deep, “true”)
  • Move & stabilise the vertebral column & head
  • Supplied by the posterior (dorsal) rami — the defining rule
Extrinsic Muscles
MuscleNerveAction
TrapeziusAccessory (CN XI) + C3–4 (proprioception)Elevates, retracts & rotates the scapula
Latissimus dorsiThoracodorsal (C6–8)Extends, adducts & medially rotates the arm (“hand in back pocket”)
Levator scapulaeDorsal scapular (C5) + C3–4Elevates the scapula
Rhomboids major & minorDorsal scapular (C4–5)Retract & rotate the scapula (glenoid down)
Serratus posterior sup./inf.Intercostal nervesAccessory muscles of respiration
The extrinsic muscles are truly limb/thoracic muscles that migrated onto the back — hence their anterior-rami (ventral) supply. The only exception to remember: trapezius is motor from the accessory nerve (CN XI).
Intrinsic Muscles — the Layers
Superficial & intermediate
  • Splenius capitis & cervicis (superficial) — bilaterally extend the head/neck; unilaterally rotate to the same side
  • Erector spinae (intermediate) — the main extensor column
Deep
  • Transversospinalis (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores) — stabilise & rotate the spine
  • Segmental: interspinales, intertransversarii, levatores costarum
Erector Spinae & Transversospinalis
Erector spinae (lateral → medial)
  • Iliocostalis (lateral) · Longissimus (intermediate) · Spinalis (medial) — “I Love Spaghetti”
  • Common tendon from the sacrum, iliac crest & lumbar spinous processes
  • Bilaterally extend the spine (maintain posture); unilaterally laterally flex
Transversospinalis
  • Run obliquely from transverse processes → spinous processes (upwards)
  • Semispinalis (spans ~6 segments), multifidus (~2–4, a key lumbar stabiliser), rotatores (1–2)
  • Extend & rotate to the opposite side
The Suboccipital Region
The four suboccipital muscles
  • Rectus capitis posterior major & minor
  • Obliquus capitis superior & inferior
  • They extend & rotate the head at the craniovertebral joints (fine postural control); supplied by the suboccipital nerve (C1 posterior ramus)
Suboccipital triangle
  • Borders: rectus capitis posterior major (medial), obliquus capitis superior (lateral), obliquus capitis inferior (inferior)
  • Contents: the vertebral artery (3rd part) & the suboccipital nerve (C1), in the sub-occipital venous plexus
The vertebral artery lies in the floor of the triangle before entering the foramen magnum — vulnerable to injury in extreme neck rotation/manipulation.
Movements of the Vertebral Column
MovementChief musclesMost in region
ExtensionErector spinae, transversospinalis, spleniusCervical & lumbar
FlexionRectus abdominis, psoas (abdominal wall)Cervical & lumbar
Lateral flexionErector spinae, quadratus lumborum, obliques (one side)Cervical & lumbar
RotationTransversospinalis, obliques; splenius (neck)Thoracic (facets) & cervical
Movement is greatest where the facets allow it: flexion/extension & lateral flexion in the mobile cervical & lumbar regions; rotation is freest in the thoracic spine (coronal facets), though limited by the ribs.
Nerve Supply & the Thoracolumbar Fascia
Intrinsic (deep) muscles = posterior (dorsal) rami — the single most testable rule.
Extrinsic muscles = anterior rami (trapezius = accessory nerve, CN XI).
Thoracolumbar fascia — encloses the deep muscles; gives attachment to latissimus dorsi & transversus abdominis, transferring load between the trunk & limb.
Multifidus is a key lumbar stabiliser — targeted in back-pain rehabilitation.
Clinical Correlations
Mechanical back strain — the commonest cause of acute back pain (erector spinae/ligamentous).
Whiplash — hyperextension/flexion straining the cervical muscles & ligaments.
Winged scapula vs a paralysed trapezius — trapezius palsy (accessory nerve, e.g. neck node biopsy) causes drooping shoulder & weak elevation.
Vertebral artery dissection — after extreme rotation/manipulation → posterior circulation stroke.
🧠 Mnemonics
Erector spinae (lateral→medial) — “I Love Spaghetti”: Iliocostalis, Longissimus, Spinalis.
Intrinsic = dorsal rami (deep & dorsal go together).
Suboccipital triangle borders — 2 obliques + rectus capitis posterior major; contents = vertebral artery + C1.
Trapezius = CN XI (the odd one out among back muscles).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Intrinsic back muscles are supplied by posterior (dorsal) rami; extrinsic by anterior rami (trapezius = CN XI).
Erector spinae = iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis (lateral→medial); the main spine extensor.
Transversospinalis (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores) run transverse→spinous and rotate contralaterally.
Splenius bilaterally extends, unilaterally rotates the head to the same side.
Suboccipital triangle: RCP major (medial), obliquus capitis superior (lateral), obliquus capitis inferior (inferior).
Suboccipital triangle contents: vertebral artery (3rd part) & suboccipital nerve (C1).
Latissimus dorsi (thoracodorsal, C6–8) = “hand in back pocket” (extend, adduct, medially rotate).
Rotation is freest in the thoracic spine; flexion/extension in the cervical & lumbar.
Multifidus is the key lumbar stabiliser.
Thoracolumbar fascia anchors latissimus dorsi & transversus abdominis.
BACK & SPINE__Spinal Cord & Meninges:
Why this matters: the spinal cord relays every sensation up and every command down, wrapped in three meninges and bathed in CSF. Learn the cord levels, the meningeal spaces, the two great sensory tracts & the corticospinal tract, and the blood supply, and lumbar puncture, cord syndromes and Brown-Séquard all fall into place.
The Spinal Cord — Overview
Extent & enlargements
  • Runs from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris (L1/L2) in adults (lower in neonates)
  • Cervical enlargement (C5–T1) — the upper limb (brachial plexus); lumbosacral enlargement (L1–S3) — the lower limb
  • Below the conus: the filum terminale (pial, anchors to the coccyx) & the cauda equina (roots)
31 pairs of spinal nerves
  • 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal
  • C1–C7 exit above their pedicle; C8 exits below C7; thereafter each nerve exits below its numbered pedicle
Internal Structure
Grey matter (central “H”/butterfly)
  • Dorsal (posterior) horn — sensory; ventral (anterior) horn — motor (LMN cell bodies)
  • Lateral horn (T1–L2) — sympathetic preganglionic neurons
White matter
  • Ascending & descending tracts in the dorsal, lateral & ventral columns (funiculi)
  • Landmarks: anterior median fissure & posterior median sulcus; a central canal (CSF)
Spinal Nerve Roots & Formation
Roots
  • Dorsal (posterior) root — sensory; its dorsal root ganglion (DRG) holds the sensory cell bodies
  • Ventral (anterior) root — motor (from the ventral horn)
  • They unite in the intervertebral foramen to form the mixed spinal nerve
Rami
  • The spinal nerve splits into a posterior (dorsal) ramus (back muscles & skin) and a larger anterior (ventral) ramus (limbs & body wall, forming plexuses)
The Meninges & Spaces
Three layers
  • Dura mater — tough outer layer (a single layer in the spine); the dural sac ends at S2
  • Arachnoid mater — deep to dura; the subarachnoid space beneath it holds CSF
  • Pia mater — clings to the cord; forms the denticulate ligaments (anchoring the cord laterally) & the filum terminale
The spaces
  • Epidural (extradural) space — outside the dura; contains fat & the internal vertebral venous (Batson’s) plexus (site of epidural anaesthesia)
  • Subdural — a potential space
  • Subarachnoid (CSF) — the lumbar cistern (L2–S2) below the conus is where CSF is sampled (LP)
Ascending (Sensory) Tracts
TractCarriesDecussates
DCML (dorsal columns)Fine touch, vibration, proprioceptionIn the medulla (internal arcuate fibres)
Spinothalamic (anterolateral)Pain, temperature, crude touchAt the cord level (within ~1–2 segments, via the anterior white commissure)
SpinocerebellarUnconscious proprioceptionTo the cerebellum (largely ipsilateral)
The where it crosses is the key to localisation: DCML crosses high (medulla), so a cord lesion gives ipsilateral loss of touch/proprioception; spinothalamic crosses low (at the cord), so the same lesion gives contralateral loss of pain/temperature — the basis of Brown-Séquard syndrome.
Descending (Motor) Tracts
Corticospinal (pyramidal)
  • Voluntary motor; ~85% decussate in the medulla (pyramids) as the lateral corticospinal tract
  • An UMN lesion (above the anterior horn) → spasticity, hyperreflexia, up-going plantars; an LMN lesion (anterior horn/root) → flaccid, wasted, areflexic
Others
  • Extrapyramidal: rubrospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, tectospinal — posture & tone
Blood Supply of the Cord
Arteries
  • One anterior spinal artery (from the vertebral arteries) — supplies the anterior ⅔ of the cord
  • Two posterior spinal arteries — the posterior ⅓ (dorsal columns)
  • Reinforced by segmental/radicular arteries; the largest is the artery of Adamkiewicz (usually left, ~T9–T12)
Watershed & venous
  • The mid-thoracic cord (~T4–T9) is a watershed zone, vulnerable to ischaemia (e.g. aortic surgery/cross-clamping)
  • Drained by anterior & posterior spinal veins → the internal vertebral venous plexus
Anterior spinal artery syndrome. Infarction of the anterior ⅔ → bilateral loss of pain/temperature & motor (spinothalamic + corticospinal) below the level, with preserved dorsal-column (touch/proprioception) function.
Cord Syndromes
Brown-Séquard (hemisection) — ipsilateral motor & dorsal-column loss + contralateral pain/temperature loss (a few levels below).
Anterior cord syndrome — loss of motor & pain/temperature, spared proprioception (ASA territory).
Central cord syndrome — upper > lower limb weakness (hyperextension in the elderly); “cape” loss in syringomyelia.
Subacute combined degeneration — B12 deficiency hits the dorsal columns & corticospinal tracts.
Tabes dorsalis — tertiary syphilis damages the dorsal columns (sensory ataxia).
Epidural haematoma / abscess — compresses the cord in the epidural space → an emergency.
🧠 Mnemonics
31 nerve pairs — 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.
DCML crosses high (medulla); spinothalamic crosses low (cord) — the key to Brown-Séquard laterality.
Anterior spinal artery = anterior ⅔; posterior spinal arteries = posterior ⅓.
Dural sac & subarachnoid space end at S2.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Cord ends at L1/L2 (conus); dural sac ends at S2; LP uses the lumbar cistern (L2–S2).
31 spinal nerve pairs (8 cervical); C8 exits below the C7 pedicle.
Lateral horn (T1–L2) = sympathetic preganglionic neurons.
DRG holds sensory cell bodies; ventral root is motor.
Epidural space contains fat & the internal vertebral venous (Batson’s) plexus.
DCML = fine touch/proprioception, decussates in the medulla; spinothalamic = pain/temp, decussates at the cord.
Corticospinal tract decussates in the medullary pyramids (~85%).
Anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior ⅔; ASA syndrome spares proprioception.
Artery of Adamkiewicz (T9–T12, usually left) is the major thoracolumbar feeder.
Brown-Séquard: ipsilateral motor/dorsal-column, contralateral pain/temperature loss.
BACK & SPINE__Vessels:
Why this matters: the spine is fed by segmental arteries at every level and drained by the valveless vertebral venous plexus of Batson — a highway for cancer to spread to bone & brain. Learn the segmental supply, the spinal-cord arteries (Adamkiewicz & the watershed) and Batson’s plexus, and cord ischaemia, spinal metastases and the vertebral artery all make sense.
Arteries of the Vertebral Column
Segmental spinal arteries by region
  • Cervical — vertebral & ascending cervical arteries
  • Thoracic — posterior intercostal arteries
  • Lumbar — lumbar arteries (from the aorta)
  • Sacral — lateral & median sacral arteries
What each segmental artery gives
  • Branches to the vertebral body & periosteum (and the muscles/skin of the back)
  • A spinal branch that enters the intervertebral foramen → supplies the vertebra & meninges, gives radicular arteries to the nerve roots, and (at some levels) a segmental medullary artery reinforcing the cord
Arterial Supply of the Spinal Cord
The three longitudinal arteries
  • One anterior spinal artery (from the two vertebral arteries) — runs in the anterior median fissure, supplying the anterior ⅔
  • Two posterior spinal arteries (from the vertebral arteries or PICA) — the posterior ⅓ (dorsal columns)
Reinforcement & the watershed
  • Segmental medullary (radicular) arteries top up the longitudinal vessels — the largest is the artery of Adamkiewicz (usually left, ~T9–T12)
  • The mid-thoracic (~T4–T9) cord is a watershed — vulnerable in aortic surgery/hypotension
Anterior spinal artery syndrome. Occlusion (e.g. aortic cross-clamp, dissection, Adamkiewicz injury) infarcts the anterior ⅔ → bilateral motor + pain/temperature loss with spared dorsal columns (proprioception).
Venous Drainage & the Vertebral Venous Plexus
The plexuses (of Batson)
  • Internal vertebral venous plexus — in the epidural space (around the dura)
  • External vertebral venous plexus — outside the vertebral column
  • They interconnect and drain via intervertebral & basivertebral veins into the segmental veins (azygos, lumbar, etc.)
Cord veins
  • Anterior & posterior spinal veins drain the cord into the internal plexus
  • Basivertebral veins emerge from the posterior vertebral body
Batson’s plexus is valveless and communicates freely with the pelvic, abdominal & thoracic veins. Raised intra-abdominal/thoracic pressure diverts blood into it — a route for prostate & breast cancer (and pelvic infection) to reach the vertebrae, pelvis & even the brain, bypassing the caval/pulmonary filter.
The Vertebral Artery
Course
  • A branch of the subclavian artery; ascends through the foramina transversaria of C6→C1
  • Passes through the suboccipital triangle and the foramen magnum to join its fellow as the basilar artery
Supplies & risks
  • Gives the anterior & posterior spinal arteries and PICA; supplies the posterior circulation of the brain
  • Dissection (neck trauma/manipulation) → posterior circulation stroke
Clinical Correlations
Spinal cord ischaemia — thoracoabdominal aortic surgery/aneurysm can occlude the artery of Adamkiewicz → paraplegia (anterior cord syndrome).
Spinal metastases — prostate & breast cancer spread via Batson’s valveless plexus to the vertebrae (a common site of bony mets).
Epidural venous engorgement in pregnancy/obesity reduces the epidural volume → less local anaesthetic needed for a block.
Vertebral artery dissection — after neck manipulation/trauma → occipital headache & brainstem/cerebellar stroke.
Epidural haematoma — bleeding from the internal vertebral plexus can compress the cord.
🧠 Mnemonics
1 anterior + 2 posterior spinal arteries; anterior ⅔ vs posterior ⅓.
Adamkiewicz — the big Anterior radicular artery, usually on the left, T9–T12.
Batson bypasses valves — valveless plexus carries cancer to the spine & brain.
Vertebral artery — up the transverse foramina C6→C1 (skips C7).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Segmental arteries: vertebral/ascending cervical (neck), posterior intercostal (thorax), lumbar (lumbar), sacral (sacrum).
Each segmental gives a spinal branch through the IV foramen → radicular arteries to the cord.
Cord: 1 anterior spinal artery (anterior ⅔), 2 posterior spinal arteries (posterior ⅓).
Artery of Adamkiewicz (usually left, T9–T12) is the major thoracolumbar feeder.
Mid-thoracic cord (~T4–T9) = watershed; anterior spinal artery syndrome spares proprioception.
Internal vertebral venous plexus lies in the epidural space; the external plexus is outside the column.
Batson’s plexus is valveless → route for prostate/breast mets to the spine & brain.
Basivertebral veins drain the vertebral body into the internal plexus.
Vertebral artery ascends the transverse foramina C6→C1 and gives the spinal arteries + PICA.
Epidural venous engorgement (pregnancy) reduces anaesthetic requirements.
